title: Supreme Court ends 60-year Bhakra-Beas dispute: Punjab, Haryana to give Himachal 11,973 MU
dek: Himachal Pradesh will get its arrears of power from the Bhakra-Nangal and Beas projects over 20 lean seasons, with its share of capital cost set off against what it is owed.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court on Friday ordered Punjab and Haryana to supply Himachal Pradesh with about 11,973 million units of electricity over the next 20 years, settling a dispute over the hill state's share of power from the Bhakra-Nangal and Beas projects that began with the reorganisation of Punjab in 1966.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said the electricity, owed to Himachal Pradesh as arrears for the decades in which it did not receive its share, would be delivered at about 598 million units a year during the lean seasons from October to March. The court disposed of the suit, which Himachal Pradesh filed in 1996, and said its 2011 ruling in the state's favour had to be carried out "without reservation".

## What the court ordered

In 2011 the Supreme Court declared that Himachal Pradesh was entitled to 7.19% of the power from the Bhakra-Nangal and Beas projects attributable to the old, undivided state of Punjab, with effect from 1 November 1966, when the Punjab Reorganisation Act came into force. Friday's judgment deals with how that decree is to be paid out.

The arrears were computed at 13,066 million units for the period from November 1966 to October 2011, reports said. One report attributed the figure to the Union government and another to the Central Electricity Authority.

Himachal Pradesh, in turn, owed its 7.19% share of the projects' capital cost. The court fixed that liability at Rs 420.77 crore and, rather than ordering cash payments in either direction, set it off against the power owed. Valuing the electricity at Rs 3.85 per unit, it adjusted about 1,093 million units against the capital-cost bill, leaving about 11,973 million units to be delivered, according to reports of the judgment.

The state will pay the charges set by the Bhakra Beas Management Board (BBMB), the body that runs the projects, for the year in which each instalment of power is received, the court directed. The settlement is to be implemented without any exchange of money.

## A longer timetable

During the hearings, Himachal Pradesh asked for the arrears to be cleared within 10 years and Punjab asked for 30, one report said. Attorney General R. Venkataramani, who led discussions between the three states, proposed 15 years. The court settled on 20, saying the longer period would ease the burden on Punjab and Haryana.

Punjab had objected that the arrears should be reduced to account for extra power it said it had already supplied to Himachal Pradesh, and that the capital cost should be computed differently. The court called those objections "vague and superficial" and an attempt to reopen issues settled by the 2011 decree, according to reports. Haryana also disputed the size of its share of the liability.

> "The directions issued by this Court are binding and are required to be acted upon without reservation." — Supreme Court, 6 November 2026

The bench also expressed frustration at the delay. "It is particularly unfortunate that a dispute which has remained pending for several decades continues to be prolonged, requiring further judicial time and attention," the court said, according to reports of the judgment. It added that a decree pending for decades "cannot be rendered fruitless by reason of the unwillingness or recalcitrance of a Judgment Debtor".

## Background

The Punjab Reorganisation Act of 1966 carved Haryana out of Punjab and transferred several hill areas, including Kangra, Kullu, Shimla and Lahaul-Spiti, to what was then the Union Territory of Himachal Pradesh, which became a full state in 1971. The Bhakra dam on the Sutlej and the Beas projects lie largely in Himachal Pradesh, and their reservoirs submerged land in the state. The Act set up a joint board, now the BBMB, to run them for the successor states.

Himachal Pradesh argued for decades that it had been denied a fair share of the power generated in its territory. It went to the Supreme Court under Article 131 of the Constitution, which gives the court original jurisdiction over disputes between the Union and states, or between states. The court ruled in the state's favour in 2011, but implementation stalled for more than a decade over how to value the arrears, which tariff to use and how much of the capital cost each state should bear.

## What they are saying

Himachal Pradesh's Public Works Minister Vikramaditya Singh told reporters in Shimla that the verdict was a "historic victory" for the state and would bring it Rs 400 crore to Rs 500 crore in additional revenue each year, one report said.

Senior advocate Kapil Sibal appeared for Himachal Pradesh. The Punjab and Haryana governments had not publicly responded to the judgment by Friday evening.

## Why it matters

For Himachal Pradesh, which earns a large part of its revenue from hydropower, the ruling turns a paper entitlement into a steady flow of electricity it can use or sell. The power will arrive in winter, when river flows and hydropower output are at their lowest.

For Punjab and Haryana, the order means giving up part of their share of BBMB power each lean season for two decades. The cashless set-off spares all three governments a large one-time payment.

The judgment also comes amid wider friction over the BBMB. Punjab and Haryana clashed publicly over water releases from the Bhakra dam in 2025.

## Key numbers

- 7.19%: Himachal Pradesh's share of Bhakra-Nangal and Beas power, decreed in 2011
- 13,066 million units: arrears for November 1966 to October 2011
- Rs 420.77 crore: Himachal Pradesh's share of capital cost, adjusted against arrears
- Rs 3.85: value per unit used for the adjustment
- About 11,973 million units: power to be supplied, at about 598 million units a year over 20 lean seasons

## What happens next

Punjab and Haryana must now arrange to deliver the first instalment during the coming lean season, which runs from October to March. The BBMB will set the charges Himachal Pradesh pays each year. The Supreme Court's order brings the 1996 suit to an end, and any dispute over implementation would have to return to the court as a fresh application.
